notes: Ruling slot 23 holds the Imbokodvo National Movement, the king's party that holds every elected seat; Sobhuza II leads it as monarch. House of Dlamini (constitutional) stays in slot 0 per MD. NNLC moved from MD slot 5 to slot 18 (has popularity; Pan-Africanist socialism fits). Swaziland has no army in 1970: slot 22 is the Royal Swaziland Police, the age regiments sit in slot 6. Tibiyo TakaNgwane (1968) in slot 15.

0.name: House of Dlamini
0.text:
The House of Dlamini is the royal clan from which every Swazi king is drawn, and its senior princes dominate both the traditional councils and the modern state. Prince Makhosini Dlamini serves as Prime Minister, while other princes hold ministries, chieftaincies and seats on the boards of the new national companies.

The modernising wing of the clan prefers to govern within the 1968 independence constitution, keep Western investors and British aid flowing and maintain correct relations with South Africa and Portuguese Mozambique. Its leverage lies in blood ties to the king and in its grip on cabinet posts, land and patronage.

1.name: Swaziland United Front
1.text:
The Swaziland United Front is a small nationalist party led by Obed Mabuza, formed by moderates who broke away from the older progressive movement in the early 1960s. It won no seats in 1964 or 1967 and survives as a modest opposition voice beside a parliament entirely held by Imbokodvo.

The Front favours constitutional government, private enterprise, Western investment and gradual Africanisation of the civil service and of land ownership, while avoiding the radical rhetoric of the Liberatory Congress. Its supporters are clerks, teachers and small businessmen in Mbabane and Manzini who want reform without upheaval.

2.name: Swaziland Progressive Party
2.text:
The Swaziland Progressive Party, founded in 1960 under John June Nquku, was the first modern political party in the territory. Weakened by repeated splits, it won no seats in 1964 or 1967 and now survives as a small opposition party still led by Nquku.

The SPP calls for one-person-one-vote democracy, a constitutional monarchy, civil liberties and an end to racial discrimination, and it seeks support from Western liberals and Commonwealth opinion. Its remaining followers are mission-educated townspeople and teachers who reject both royal absolutism and the radicalism of the Liberatory Congress.

3.name: Swaziland National Association of Teachers
3.text:
The Swaziland National Association of Teachers is the country's largest organised profession and one of the few bodies with members in every district. Founded in the colonial period, it represents the mission and government teachers who staff the expanding school system and form much of the educated African middle class.

Its leaders press for better salaries, Africanisation of education, free speech and collective bargaining for public servants, and lean toward social-democratic reform within the constitutional order. Its leverage lies in the classroom: teachers shape opinion in the villages and supply much of the opposition's activist base.

4.name: South African Communist Party
4.text:
The South African Communist Party, driven underground in its own country, uses Swaziland as a quiet transit route and refuge for its cadres. Its members in the kingdom are few, mostly exiles, sympathetic teachers and a handful of workers, and they operate under the watch of the Royal Swaziland Police and South African agents.

The SACP is firmly pro-Soviet, works in alliance with the African National Congress and seeks the overthrow of apartheid through mass struggle and armed action. In Swaziland its leverage lies in secret networks and safe houses and in the hope of politicising the workers of the mines and sugar estates.

5.name: Umkhonto we Sizwe
5.text:
Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the African National Congress founded in 1961, uses Swaziland as a corridor between South Africa and the camps in Tanzania and Zambia. Its operatives in the kingdom are a handful of couriers, refugees and recruits moving at night along the mountain border.

MK preaches armed revolution against apartheid and enjoys Soviet and East German backing, but in Swaziland it cannot act openly against a government determined to stay on good terms with Pretoria. Its leverage lies in sympathy among young Swazi radicals and in its power to draw the kingdom into the regional conflict.

6.name: Emabutfo
6.text:
The emabutfo are the age regiments of the Swazi nation, called up by the king for royal ceremonies, communal labour on the royal fields and, in earlier times, for war. Every generation of young men is enrolled in one, and the regiments gather in force at the Incwala and other national rites.

Their hardline elders regard political parties, the Westminster constitution and Western manners as alien to Swazi custom and want the king to rule as his ancestors did. Suspicious of white settlers and concessionaires, they form the muscle of royal traditionalism, and their leverage lies in thousands of disciplined men who answer only to the Ngwenyama.

7.name: Tinsizwa TeNkhululeko
7.text:
Tinsizwa TeNkhululeko, 'the Young Men of Freedom', are radical Liberatory Congress youths and returnees from Dar es Salaam and Lusaka who have concluded that elections will never dislodge the royal establishment. They admire the single-party states of independent Africa and the discipline of the liberation movements.

They want a revolutionary one-party state, the expulsion of British and South African influence from the police and economy, and nationalisation of the mines and estates with help from the Eastern bloc and China. Their leverage lies among unemployed young men in Manzini and the labour compounds, and in contacts with the guerrilla networks crossing the kingdom.

8.name: Idara-e-Jafaria
8.text:
Idara-e-Jafaria is a small Shia welfare and study circle among Indian-origin trading families in Manzini and Mbabane, part of the Khoja diaspora that stretches from Durban to Zanzibar. It gathers in a family house for Muharram majalis and lessons for the children.

Its members favour an educated, reform-minded Shia faith that values schooling, charity and good relations with the authorities. Politically cautious, they seek security for their shops and freedom of worship from the king's government, and they look for guidance to the seminaries of Najaf and to the larger Khoja jamaats of East Africa.

9.name: Anjuman-e-Panjtani
9.text:
Anjuman-e-Panjtani is a handful of zealous young Shia men in Manzini who returned from religious study in Iraq and Pakistan convinced that their elders have grown too comfortable. They meet apart from the main community, around cassette sermons and pamphlets from Najaf and Qom.

They insist that only the learned clergy may guide Muslim life, condemn the Shah of Iran and the Western powers that back him, and want strict religious discipline among the faithful. Without numbers or legal standing in a Christian kingdom, their leverage is confined to a few households and to ties with militant clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Jamaat-e-Manzini
10.text:
Jamaat-e-Manzini is the Sunni congregation of Swaziland, made up of Indian-origin traders, Malawian and Mozambican migrant workers and a few Swazi converts who pray in the small mosque at Manzini. Its imams are trained in Natal and follow the conservative ulama of the subcontinent.

The community is loyal and quietist, accepting the authority of the king and asking only for freedom of worship, Muslim schooling and land for burial grounds. It receives charity from Durban and the Gulf, and its leverage lies in the commerce of its traders and in the respect it has earned for keeping clear of politics.

11.name: Halqat al-Khilafa
11.text:
Halqat al-Khilafa is a tiny clandestine circle of young Muslims in Manzini and the railway and mining settlements who have come across Hizb ut-Tahrir literature through contacts in Durban and London. It has no public existence and meets in back rooms.

Its members reject monarchy, parliament and both superpowers as man-made orders and call for a single caliphate uniting all Muslims. In Swaziland they can do little beyond reading circles and recruitment among migrant workers, but they see themselves as part of a coming worldwide revival that will erase the borders drawn by the colonial powers.

12.name: Usrat al-Ikhwan
12.text:
Usrat al-Ikhwan is a study group of educated young Muslims in Mbabane and Manzini, teachers, clerks and students, who read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in English and look to Muslim youth movements in South Africa and abroad for inspiration. They want an active, organised Islam engaged with society.

The group promotes Islamic education, welfare work and moral reform, accepts constitutional politics and speaks out for Palestine and for Africa's poor. Neutral between the blocs, it hopes to give Muslims a voice in national life, though its leverage remains limited to classrooms, a reading room and a small network of families.

13.name: Swazi National Council
13.text:
The Swazi National Council is the traditional assembly of Swazi men under the king, steered in practice by its inner standing committee, the Liqoqo, of princes, chiefs and royal advisers. It sits beside the parliament created by the 1968 constitution and controls Swazi Nation Land, custom and royal revenue.

The Council's leaders see Westminster institutions as a foreign graft and want decisions taken through consultation at the royal residences rather than in party debate. Neutral between the blocs, they prize order, hierarchy and royal authority, and their leverage lies in land: whoever farms Swazi Nation Land does so by their leave.

14.name: Tikhulu
14.text:
Tikhulu, 'the Chiefs', are the territorial chiefs who govern the rural Swazi through their royal kraals, allocate land, try local disputes and mobilise villagers for the king's fields. Many owe their positions to royal favour and serve as the eyes and ears of the monarchy in the countryside.

They stand for homestead farming, cattle, custom and the authority of elders, and are wary of townspeople, trade unions and political parties alike. Neutral in the Cold War and wary of foreign ideas, they want development that leaves their authority intact, and their leverage lies in controlling who receives land and who is heard at court.

15.name: Tibiyo TakaNgwane
15.text:
Tibiyo TakaNgwane was created by royal charter in 1968 as a national fund held in trust by King Sobhuza II for the Swazi nation, receiving mineral royalties and taking stakes in companies. Run by royal appointees outside parliamentary control, it is the vehicle through which the crown joins the British and South African firms that dominate sugar, timber, asbestos and iron ore.

Its managers want partnership with foreign capital rather than nationalisation, returns invested at the king's discretion and no scrutiny from politicians. Their leverage lies in mining royalties, growing shareholdings and the ability to reward loyal princes and chiefs with board seats.

16.name: Bahwebi BaseManzini
16.text:
Bahwebi BaseManzini, 'the Traders of Manzini', are Swazi shopkeepers, bus owners, butchers and market traders who want to break into a commerce long controlled by European and Indian firms and by the big concession companies. Manzini's busy market is their stronghold.

They call for easy trading licences, lower duties, cheap credit for African business and less interference from both royal officials and the state, and they oppose nationalisation as firmly as they oppose monopoly. Their leverage lies in the transport and retail networks that link the towns to the countryside and in the growing class of Swazi entrepreneurs.

17.name: Bavikeli Bemvelo
17.text:
Bavikeli Bemvelo, 'the Protectors of Nature', is a circle of conservationists, wildlife rangers and farmers around Ted Reilly, who turned his family farm into the Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary in 1961 to save antelope and other animals nearly wiped out by hunting and settlement. They have won the interest of King Sobhuza II for their cause.

They campaign against poaching and the destruction of forests and grasslands by plantations and overgrazing, and want new reserves in the lowveld and mountains. Their leverage lies in the king's patronage, international conservation contacts and the promise that wildlife tourism can bring revenue to a small country.

18.name: Ngwane National Liberatory Congress
18.text:
The Ngwane National Liberatory Congress was founded in 1963 by Dr Ambrose Zwane after splits in the progressive movement and is the main opposition to royal rule. It played a leading part in the strikes of 1963 and took about a fifth of the vote in 1967 without winning a single seat.

The NNLC is Pan-Africanist and socialist, calling for a strictly constitutional monarchy, non-racial democracy, land reform and fair wages on the mines and estates, and solidarity with the liberation movements. Its strength lies among workers, teachers and townspeople in Manzini and Mbabane, especially in constituencies where wage labour has loosened chiefly control.

19.name: Pan Africanist Congress
19.text:
The Pan Africanist Congress, banned in South Africa since 1960, keeps a small underground presence in Swaziland among refugees, students and sympathisers in the Liberatory Congress. Its external leadership under Potlako Leballo operates from Dar es Salaam, and its cadres use the kingdom as a passage to and from the Republic.

The PAC rejects multiracial liberalism and Moscow-aligned communism alike, preaches an Africanist armed struggle and increasingly looks to Maoist China for training and support. In Swaziland its leverage lies in personal ties to radical Congress members and its ability to recruit among frustrated young men in the border towns.

20.name: Umhlaba WaKaNgwane
20.text:
Umhlaba WaKaNgwane, 'the Land of Ngwane', is a populist current of chiefs, royalist politicians and landless homesteaders obsessed with the land lost to European concessionaires under the partition of 1907, which left much of the country in settler and company hands. They also claim the Swazi-speaking districts left inside South Africa.

They demand the buying back or seizure of settler farms, restrictions on foreign landowners and traders, and preference for Swazis in jobs and licences. Hostile to both liberal reformers and socialists, they rally rural crowds with a simple promise, and their leverage lies in a grievance felt in nearly every homestead.

21.name: Die Grensboere
21.text:
Die Grensboere, 'the Border Farmers', are hardline Afrikaner and other white settler farmers of the Swazi highveld and lowveld who never accepted majority rule and look across the border to the National Party government in Pretoria. Some keep membership in South African organisations and rifle clubs.

They want settler title to land guaranteed forever, an end to talk of land redistribution, and Swaziland bound tightly to the apartheid republic, with African politics kept firmly in check. Few in number, their leverage lies in their farms, their weapons and their connections to South African security services that watch the kingdom closely.

22.name: Royal Swaziland Police
22.text:
The Royal Swaziland Police is the kingdom's only modern armed force, since independent Swaziland has no army. Built under British rule and still partly led by expatriate officers, it includes a paramilitary mobile unit and remembers the strikes of 1963, when British troops had to be flown in to restore order.

Its senior officers are loyal to the king and see themselves as the guardians of stability against strikes, radical parties and guerrilla infiltration from South Africa and Mozambique. Their leverage lies in a monopoly of rifles, vehicles and radios and in the Special Branch files kept on every opposition figure.

23.name: Imbokodvo National Movement
23.text:
The Imbokodvo National Movement, 'the Grindstone', was founded in 1964 on the initiative of King Sobhuza II to carry royal and traditional authority into modern party politics. It swept every elected seat in 1964 and again in 1967, and since independence on 6 September 1968 it governs with Prince Makhosini Dlamini as Prime Minister.

Imbokodvo stands for the supremacy of the Ngwenyama, Swazi custom and the Swazi National Council, the recovery of land lost to concessionaires, and cautious development with Western and South African capital. Its leverage is total: parliament, chiefs, regiments and the king's own authority all run through it.
